doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Optimism and cynicism about America
summary: He is personally optimistic but cynical, citing de Tocqueville, neglect of the common good and problems like racism and weak education.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Are you optimistic about the country addressing some of those things that you mentioned in the past?

I’m personally optimistic but I’m secretly cynical — not pessimistic, just cynical — in the sense that for so long de Tocqueville really had it right when he talked about some of the failings of our country, one of them being that we like to put our head in the sand whenever we confront a serious quote problem unquote that we tend to want to run away from it. And we want to renounce things that are American. We’re so busy inventing things and constructing things that we just do it and then walk away from it without trying to learn the lessons of it. Whether they succeed or fail, I mean we don’t learn either way. I mean it’s a particularly American kind of trait. Because we’re so busy creating, so busy going on to the next signpost that we never — one thing, we never — we don’t like to look behind us to see what’s really going on, we don’t like to study what we’re going at the moment when we do it. I mean these are things that democracy in America, I mean we’re talking early nineteenth century here, this guy busted us for that and we haven’t really gotten out of any of that. It appears that things like the common good, the public welfare, those concepts are really dead now. It seems also that the protection of the public from the tyrannies of corporate greed, the tyrannies of market manipulation, the tyrannies of the lack of consumer protection and the lack of environmental protection, I mean all of those things and then this has nothing to do with the current political regime. It has all to do with things that have actually gone on since the end of the Johnson administration. I mean I’m really arguing that it started long before that but the point I’m trying to raise here in that this is not something that’s either a democratic or a republican kind of problem that has been one party or the other that’s been responsible for all this scalawags

running around here today. But it’s just that there has been an undeniable drift to neglecting the real problems that exist in our country at the moment. Racism is an obvious one. Sexism and classism, those are obvious. But things that aren’t so obvious, you know, the denial of basic education to everybody, and it doesn’t matter whether you’ve coming from a public school district that has a lot of money or a public school district that doesn’t have very much money. I can tell you, and actually I don’t have to tell you because you see it too, the kind of students that we’re getting from these school systems, it’s unbelievable. I mean now I’ve been gone 25 years. And I finished my first semester, and I’m looking at these papers coming in—
